tagline.text: Rice terraces, Bohol's tallest waterfall and mangroves in an eastern town

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Candijay, Bohol (about 97 km east of Tagbilaran)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–2,500 (full day, covering transport, fees and lunch; rental car not included)

children.text: Candijay is a municipality on Bohol's eastern coast, and the Cadapdapan rice terraces, Can-umantad Falls and Canawa Cold Spring combine into one good day trip. It is about 97 km from Tagbilaran, so plan an early start.
Candijay is a municipality on the eastern coast of Bohol, about
97 km
from the provincial capital, Tagbilaran. It sits on Cogtong Bay and borders Alicia, Mabini and Pilar, with Anda also nearby. It covers about
103 km²

and had roughly 30,100 residents in the 2024 census. While most visitors to Bohol circle Panglao in the west and the Chocolate Hills in the center, this eastern town fills a day with quieter, more rural scenery.

The face of Candijay is the rice terraces of the village of Cadapdapan. The paddies step up the mountainside, and the same river flows down to Can-umantad Falls. According to the Bohol tourism office, the falls drop about

and are called the tallest in Bohol; the terraces were made long ago by villagers who turned high ground into farmland, and the golden color of ripening rice is regarded as wealth inherited from their ancestors. The terraces and the falls are about a
15-minute

walk apart, so see them together. One travel blog says you can visit all three places (terraces, falls and cold spring) in a single day and that each entrance fee is very low. The roads are a mix of paved and unpaved, so it helps to save the location on Google Maps beforehand.

Wikipedia also lists other attractions: Canawa Cold Spring, the Kawasihan sandbar off Panas, caves (Layog Cave in Luan, Sangat Cave in Tambongan and Ilaja Cave in Panas), Danicop Gorge Brook, Kantaligsok Peak, and the Candijay mangrove forest in Panadtaran with its mangrove adventure tour. Many of these are adventurous, but how developed and how accessible they are varies a lot from place to place, so it is realistic to build your first itinerary around the terraces, the falls and the cold spring.

The name Candijay is said to come from "Kang Dihay," meaning "belonging to Dihay," a leader and his followers. The town was organized in the Spanish period and was recorded as one of Bohol's 34 towns in 1879; the parish church is dedicated to St. Joseph, whose feast day is
May 19

. It is a 3rd-class municipality and has not yet been developed for mass tourism, so use the municipal tourism office and local guides when you need help or information. If you are wondering whether to include Candijay, here is a way to decide. If you have already seen the Panglao beaches, the Chocolate Hills and the Loboc River and want quieter natural scenery, it is a good choice. If travel time is a burden or you prefer well-equipped sightseeing, a Panglao-area itinerary is better. Allow about 3–4 hours of round-trip travel alone, so clear a whole day.

Paddies laid out in tiers on the mountainside in the village of Cadapdapan, turning golden as they ripen and light green at planting time. You can walk the narrow paddy paths for photos and rest at a farm restaurant nearby. One travel account compares them to the Tegallalang rice terraces in Bali but with far fewer people. You register at the village entrance, and many visitors use one farm restaurant as a base, leaving their bags there while they look around. The paddy paths are narrow and can be slippery, so sneakers or sandals with good grip are best.
A two-tier waterfall with a drop of about
and a deep pool below that you can swim in. You can walk down from the restaurant by the terraces in about
15 minutes

, or ride a motorcycle down a steep paved road. Can-umantad Falls is also covered in its own entry. Accounts differ on the height, with one source giving the main cascade as about 45 feet, so expect the experience rather than a particular number.

A round natural pool in the forest whose bottom has never been reached, they say. Concrete walls and steps at the entrance let non-swimmers, children included, play at the edge. The name is said to come from the local word "cawa," meaning a pan. The water is cold and clear, good for cooling off at midday on a hot day, and the entrance fee is small even if you visit on the same day as the falls.

A mangrove forest in Panadtaran where a local association runs a mangrove adventure tour. The scenery changes with the tide, so check the tide when you book. Mangroves protect the coast and shelter fish and crabs, so do not step on the roots or break branches, and follow your guide's instructions.
A small islet and sandbar off Panas. Access and fees are not fixed, so ask the municipal tourism office and arrange a boat. The sandbar changes with the tide, so check the tide before you go.
Layog Cave, Sangat Cave, Ilaja Cave and the Danicop Gorge brook are for adventurous travelers. They require safety gear and a local guide, so do not go alone.

The poblacion has the St. Joseph parish church, a market and restaurants. It is a good place to have lunch during a tour or buy any water you need. Around the church's feast day (St. Joseph, May 19) the town holds a fiesta and the mood is lively.
Set out from Panglao or Tagbilaran. One record says it takes about
2 hours
by motorcycle from Panglao.
Arrive at the Candijay poblacion, buy water and snacks, and find a habal-habal.
Go up to the Cadapdapan rice terraces, register at the village, and walk the paddy paths.
Rest at the restaurant by the terraces, then walk down to Can-umantad Falls for a swim.
Come back down to the poblacion for lunch.
Swim at Canawa Cold Spring and get ready for the trip back.
The return to Tagbilaran is long, so it is safer to leave before dark. If time is short, skip the cold spring and concentrate on the terraces and falls.
See the terraces and falls in Candijay first.
After lunch, move on to neighboring Anda.
Spend the afternoon at the beach and the cave pool in Anda.
There are direct flights from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG). Airlines and schedules change, so check when you book.
You can also go through Cebu and take a high-speed ferry to Tagbilaran.
Check the latest announcements for flight and ferry schedules.
Take a bus or van from the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal heading to Jagna or Ubay and get off at Lungsoda-an or the Candijay poblacion. In 2019 the van fare was ₱130.
The bus can take about twice as long as the van. Candijay is more than 100 km away, so take the first trip of the day or rent a vehicle.
Charter a habal-habal from the highway and you reach the terrace entrance in about
15 minutes
. In 2019 the round-trip fare was ₱300.
With a rental car or a car and driver, it is easy to cover the falls and the cold spring in one day.
The
December–May
dry season is best for planning, and the greenest and the golden stages of the rice vary from year to year, so ask locally before you go.
The falls and the cold spring swell after rain and the paths turn slippery, so leave extra time in the rainy season.

Mornings are best. Early in the day, mist and sunlight spread over the terraces and make good photos, while midday is hot with little shade. Swim at the falls around midday when you are warm, and because you will have to think about the long way back later, finish before
. Weekends bring more local families and are busier, so weekdays are quieter.

Candijay town has small lodgings and shops, but most travelers set out from Panglao or Tagbilaran in the morning and return in the evening, or stay in Anda. Anda is a resort area on the eastern coast close to Candijay, with several beach resorts. Restaurants and shops cluster near the market in town, so if you arrive early in the morning it is easy to buy water and snacks.

By the terraces there are farm restaurants where you can rest with a view and have local dishes for lunch. In town you can find Bohol home cooking such as rice dishes, grilled fish and roast chicken, and you should buy water and snacks before heading to the falls.

If you plan two days on the eastern coast, a common order is to see the terraces and falls in Candijay on the first day, move to Anda for the night, and enjoy the Anda beach and cave pool on the second day. Dinner choices in Anda may be fewer than in Panglao, so check in advance whether your lodging serves meals.
Start early in the morning so you can see the terraces and falls and still get back before dark.
Carry plenty of cash in small bills. Entrance fees and habal-habal rides are all paid in cash.
Bring swimwear, a towel, water shoes and a change of clothes.
Agree with your habal-habal driver in advance on waiting for you during the round trip.
For coastal sites such as the mangroves and the sandbar, check the tide.
Contact the municipal tourism office (Candijay Tourism) for the latest fees and hours.
The falls are said to be open from
to
, but confirm this locally.
If you plan to ride a motorcycle yourself, do so only if you are experienced, given the unpaved sections and steep slopes.
There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat and sunscreen.
When taking photos near the terraces, do not walk into the paddies or step on the crops, so you do not disturb the people farming.
The road down to the falls is very steep and slippery in the rain. If you ride down on a motorcycle, choose an experienced driver.
Some of the pools at the falls and the cold spring are deep and hard to swim in without a life jacket.
Do not enter the caves and gorge without a guide.
Fees and hours change easily, so check the latest information.
The distances are long, so watch for drowsy driving and avoid traveling at night.
In the rainy season dirt roads turn muddy, which makes motorcycles dangerous.
Many paddies are private land worked by farmers, so do not enter without permission.
A tall waterfall about a
15-minute
walk from the terraces.
A resort town on the eastern coast southeast of Candijay, with beaches and a cave pool.
Bohol's signature sight in the center of the island, and many visitors continue there on a similar regional itinerary.
